title: Service necessity: Verifiability cannot ensure proper treatment
desc: Contrasts restrictive honest-service theory with laboratory and field evidence showing that observability and lower prices need not reduce fraud.

kps.k: The cluster frames expert services as a problem of judging necessity and suitability, not merely observing delivered work.
kps.d: Credence-goods research distinguishes insufficient service, unnecessarily costly service and billing for work not delivered. Successful service need not establish that it was necessary; accurate billing need not establish that it was appropriate. Mistreatment wastes resources, while overcharging initially transfers income but can also deter beneficial purchases. Balafoutas and Kerschbamer’s review and Liu and Ma explicitly include legal services as motivating examples, but the supplied evidence does not measure misconduct in legal or AI-assisted services.

kps.k: The benchmark theory permits honest, efficient service, but only under specific institutional and pricing conditions.
kps.d: Dulleck and Kerschbamer require homogeneous customers, commitment following diagnosis and either liability against insufficient treatment or verifiability of delivered treatment. With verifiability alone, equal absolute markups remove treatment-selection incentives; with liability alone, uniform treatment prices remove billing and overtreatment incentives. Their claim therefore rejects information asymmetry as a sufficient explanation of fraud, not the need for safeguards. Relaxing customer homogeneity, commitment or both safeguards can produce exclusion, duplicated diagnosis, mistreatment or market collapse. Observable costs and perfect diagnosis further restrict the benchmark.

kps.k: The laboratory evidence challenges the theoretical equivalence of liability and verifiability.
kps.d: Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter’s 936-participant factorial experiment separately varies liability, verifiability, reputation and competition. Liability strongly increases trade and efficiency; verifiability has only a minor effect despite the standard model’s prediction. Liability prevents undertreatment by experimental design, but leaves observed overtreatment and overcharging unchanged. The authors favour liability clauses among the tested remedies. The later review qualifies any universal ranking: heterogeneous preferences and unobserved expert costs undermine benchmark predictions, and alternative models rank safeguards differently across parameter settings.

qs.q: More precisely, we have examined in a 2×2×2×2 experimental design the role of liability, verifiability, reputation, or competition.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

qs.q: Their main finding is that under the liability assumption the market outcome is more efficient than under the verifiability assumption when the problem associated with the greater surplus is sufficiently more likely, while the opposite relationship might hold for other parameter constellations.
qs.a: Credence Goods in the Literature: What the Past Fifteen Years Have Taught Us about Fraud, Incentives, and the Role of Institutions · Academia · 2020

kps.k: Lower prices, greater trade and stronger reputation do not necessarily mean less fraud or higher efficiency.
kps.d: The factorial experiment finds that competition lowers prices and raises transactions without changing misconduct rates. Its abstract and conclusion qualify the efficiency result differently—by liability and by a verifiability exception—so neither supports an unconditional efficiency gain. Balafoutas and Kerschbamer also report a different experiment in which endogenous price competition increases under- and overtreatment. Their review finds no systematic fraud-reducing effect from reputation. Hidden misconduct offers one explanation for weak reputational discipline; isolated benefits, including reduced overcharging in the factorial experiment, do not establish a general remedy.

qs.q: to say that competition solves all the problems on credence goods markets, because we have also found that the likelihood of undertreatment, overtreatment, or overcharging, is not reduced (but interestingly not increased either) through seller competition.
qs.a: The Economics of Credence Goods: An Experiment on the Role of Liability, Verifiability, Reputation, and Competition · Academia · 2011

kps.k: Field studies establish setting-specific misconduct, while behavioural evidence complicates purely financial explanations.
kps.d: The review reports unnecessary repairs in more than half of Schneider’s undercover car-repair visits, detours by about 45% of sampled taxi drivers in Balafoutas et al. and suitable insurance recommendations as low as 5% in Anagol et al.’s Indian setting. These are not a common fraud rate or independent replications of the laboratory study. In that laboratory study, experts provide appropriate treatment in about half of cases even under the least protective conditions, and a model incorporating non-financial preferences generally fits better. The review adds evidence on promises and physician altruism, but also theoretical cases where conscientious experts coexist with greater aggregate fraud.

qs.q: We start the conclusion by noting that even under the most disadvantageous market conditions for consumers the sellers of credence goods have provided an appropriate treatment in about half of the cases in our experiment.

kps.k: More information and second opinions can improve discipline, but can also change incentives in adverse ways.
kps.d: The review describes models and laboratory evidence in which experts target better-informed, high-risk customers, alongside possible unintended consequences of commission disclosure. Second opinions can deter fraud, but can duplicate diagnostic costs or induce experts to conceal information to prevent shopping and advice free-riding. A reviewed dental field study finds only an insignificant decline in overtreatment from 29% to 27%. Separately, Liu and Ma’s continuous-loss model yields inefficient equilibria even when consumers infer losses precisely; when experts instead choose their information structure, a binary signal achieves the first best. That conditional theoretical result does not establish that less information generally improves services.

kps.k: Practical remedies must separately address diagnosis, truthful recommendations, adequate delivery and honest billing.
kps.d: The review stresses that equal markups can remove incentives to misreport without rewarding costly, hidden diagnostic effort. Separating diagnosis from treatment can reduce sales conflicts, but collusion or lost economies of scope can offset the benefit; carefully structured payments matter. Diagnostic uncertainty also increases fraud and reduces entry in a reviewed laboratory study, lowering efficiency by about 16%. The practical implication for applying this framework to legal services is to ask which failure a safeguard addresses: documenting work does not prove its necessity, and checking AI output is not the same institution as verifiability of billed treatment. The sources support context-sensitive design, not a tested legal-AI prescription.

vlens.an: The selected academia and research sources accept the proposition that observing or documenting delivered work does not by itself establish that the service was necessary or suitable. Collectively, they materially develop it by separating treatment adequacy, billing accuracy, diagnostic effort and outcome responsibility as distinct incentive problems. The principal internal variation concerns when verifiability can nevertheless support honest service: the benchmark theory permits this under restrictive assumptions—including homogeneous consumers, commitment and incentive-compatible pricing—whereas the laboratory experiment finds verifiability only weakly effective relative to liability. The later review explains this gap through heterogeneous motivations, hidden costs and diagnostic incentives, while Liu and Ma further show theoretically that even precise inference can coexist with inefficient outcomes. These sources therefore support context-sensitive institutional design rather than a universal claim that verifiability is useless. Because the corpus is curated, this characterises these sources only and not academia or researchers generally.

elens.an: The pre-2015 foundation sources support the proposition that observing or documenting delivered work cannot by itself ensure that the treatment was necessary or suitable. Both distinguish verifiability of what was supplied or billed from the consumer’s ability to judge whether that service was appropriate. Material variation lies between theory and experiment: Dulleck and Kerschbamer provide a restrictive benchmark in which verifiability can sustain honest, efficient service when combined with homogeneous consumers, commitment and incentive-compatible pricing; Dulleck, Kerschbamer and Sutter’s laboratory experiment then finds that verifiability has only a minor effect, while liability more strongly improves trade and efficiency. This is not opposition to the proposition, because the theoretical result is conditional rather than a claim that verifiability generally guarantees proper treatment. These curated sources establish conceptual and experimental foundations, not direct evidence about legal or AI-assisted services.

elens.an: The supplied 2020 review accepts the proposition that observing or verifying delivered work cannot by itself establish whether the service was necessary or suitable. It materially develops that proposition in three ways: it distinguishes overcharging, which verifiability directly prevents, from under- and overtreatment, which remain possible; it reports laboratory evidence in which verifiability had at most a minor effect while liability had a crucial effect; and it explains that favourable theoretical results depend on restrictive assumptions about pricing, commitment, customer homogeneity and expert costs. Internal variation lies mainly in the conditional theory: verifiability can support honest service under equal mark-ups and benchmark assumptions, and its performance relative to liability can vary by parameter setting. That qualification does not reverse the source’s overall alignment with the proposition. Because the evidence consists of one curated review, this assessment characterises that source rather than the wider 2015–2022 literature.

qs.q: Under verifiability (but without liability) the overcharging problem is eliminated more or less by definition, but the problems of under- and overtreatment are still present.

elens.an: The sole curated source from 2023–2024 accepts and materially extends the proposition through a richer theoretical model of credence goods. It shows that precise consumer inference does not by itself ensure efficient or appropriate service: even separating equilibria leave some beneficial repairs undone. It also sharpens the institutional distinction between verifiability—requiring the expert to perform promised work—and liability for eliminating the underlying loss, directly supporting the proposition that observable delivery cannot establish treatment necessity or suitability. The main internal qualification is that inefficiency is not inevitable under every information regime: when the expert can choose an information structure, a binary signal can achieve the first best. That conditional result develops the cluster’s context-sensitive account of information rather than contradicting it. The analysis is theoretical, with legal services used only as a motivating example; it does not provide empirical evidence about legal or AI-assisted services.
